Course Content.UNIT III: Centre-State Relations: Centre-State Relations; Legislative Relations; Administrative Relations; Financial Relations; Cooperation between Centre and States; Coordination between Centre and States; Judicial Interpretation of Centre-State Relations; Constitutional Doctrines evolved by Judiciary

syllabus.Course Objectives: CO1: To introduce students to the structure, powers and functions of constitutional organs under the Indian Constitution. CO2: To examine the constitutional framework relating to legislature, executive and judiciary in India. CO3: To analyze Centre-State relations and constitutional distribution of powers in the federal system. CO4: To understand constitutional provisions relating to emergency powers, state liability and public services. CO5: To familiarize students with constitutional amendments, judicial doctrines and the Basic Structure Theory.
syllabus.Suggested Readings: M.P. Jain – Indian Constitutional Law; V.N. Shukla – Constitution of India; Granville Austin – Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation; H.M. Seervai – Constitutional Law of India; G.C.V. Subba Rao – Indian Constitutional Law; B. Shiva Rao – Framing of India’s Constitution; J.N. Pandey – Constitutional Law of India; D.D. Basu – Introduction to the Constitution of India; M.P. Singh – V.N. Shukla’s Constitution of India; H.R. Khanna – Making of India’s Constitutio
syllabus.Suggested Case Laws: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala; S.R. Bommai v Union of India; Minerva Mills v Union of India; Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain; ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla; Shamsher Singh v State of Punjab; Union of India v H.S. Dhillon; State of Rajasthan v Union of India; I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu; Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu
syllabus.Course Learning Outcomes: CO1: Explain the constitutional structure and functioning of legislature, executive and judiciary in India. CO2: Analyze constitutional provisions relating to powers, privileges and accountability of constitutional authorities. CO3: Examine Centre-State relations and constitutional doctrines evolved through judicial interpretation. CO4: Apply constitutional principles relating to emergency powers, state liability and public services in legal contexts. CO5: Evaluate constitutional amendments, federalism and judicial doctrines including the Basic Structure Theory.

Course Content.UNIT I: Introduction to Public International Law: Definition of International Law; Nature of International Law; Scope and Importance of International Law; Relation between International Law and Municipal Law; Sources of International Law; Codification of International Law
Course Content.UNIT V: International Organizations: League of Nations; United Nations Organization; International Court of Justice (ICJ); International Criminal Court (ICC); Specialized Agencies of the United Nations; WHO; UNESCO; ILO; IMF; WTO
Course Content.UNIT II: States and International Responsibility: State Recognition; State Succession; Responsibility of States for International Delinquencies; State Territory; Modes of Acquisition of State Territory
Course Content.UNIT IV: International Legal Regimes: Law of the Sea: Evolution of the Law of the Sea; Freedoms of the High Seas; Common Heritage of Mankind; United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Air Law: Legal Regime of Airspace; Paris Convention; Havana Convention; Warsaw Convention; Chicago Convention; Five Freedoms of Air. Outer Space Law: Legal Regime of Outer Space; Outer Space Treaty; Agreement on Rescue and Return of Astronauts; Liability Convention; Agreement on Registration of Space Objects; Moon Treaty; UNISPACE; Recent Developments in India’s Space Missions
Course Content.UNIT III: Individuals and Treaties in International Law: Position of Individual in International Law; Nationality; Extradition; Asylum; Privileges and Immunities of Diplomatic Envoys; Treaties; Formation of Treaties; Modes of Consent; Reservation to Treaties; Termination of Treaties

syllabus.Course Objectives: CO1: To introduce students to the nature, sources and development of Public International Law. CO2: To explain the legal principles governing states, recognition, territory and international responsibility. CO3: To examine the rights and duties of individuals and states under international law. CO4: To familiarize students with international legal regimes relating to sea, air and outer space. CO5: To develop understanding of international organizations and dispute resolution mechanisms in international law.
syllabus.Suggested Readings: J.G. Starke – Introduction to International Law; J.L. Brierly – The Law of Nations; Ian Brownlie – Principles of Public International Law; S.K. Kapoor – Public International Law; H.O. Agarwal – International Law and Human Rights; S.K. Verma – An Introduction to Public International Law; Malcolm N. Shaw – International Law; Oppenheim – International Law; V.D. Mahajan – International Law; UNCLOS and Vienna Convention on Law of Treaties (Reference Material)
syllabus.Suggested Case Laws: Lotus Case; North Sea Continental Shelf Cases; Corfu Channel Case; Nicaragua v United States; Asylum Case; Nottebohm Case; Barcelona Traction Case; SS Wimbledon Case; Arrest Warrant Case; South China Sea Arbitration Case
syllabus.Course Learning Outcomes: CO1: Explain the concepts, nature and sources of Public International Law. CO2: Analyze legal principles relating to statehood, recognition and international responsibility. CO3: Examine international legal rules governing nationality, extradition, asylum and treaties. CO4: Apply international legal principles relating to sea, airspace and outer space regimes. CO5: Evaluate the role of international organizations and international adjudicatory institutions.

Course Content.UNIT I: Introduction to Administrative Law: Nature of Administrative Law; Scope of Administrative Law; Meaning and Definition of Administrative Law; Evolution of Administrative Law; Reasons for Growth of Administrative Law; Relationship between Administrative Law and Constitutional Law
Course Content.UNIT V: Remedies and Administrative Institutions: Remedies against the State; Constitutional Writs; Lokpal and Lokayukta; Liability of State in Torts; Liability of State in Contracts; Rule of Promissory Estoppel; Administrative Tribunals; Commissions of Inquiry; Public Corporations
Course Content.UNIT II: Basic Concepts of Administrative Law: Rule of Law; Dicey’s Principle of Rule of Law; Modern Trends in Rule of Law; Theory of Separation of Powers; Position in India; Position in United Kingdom; Position in United States of America
Course Content.UNIT IV: Judicial Control of Administrative Action: Judicial Control of Administrative Action; Grounds of Judicial Review; Principles of Natural Justice; Administrative Discretion; Control of Administrative Discretion; Wednesbury Principle; Doctrine of Proportionality; Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation
Course Content.UNIT III: Administrative Functions and Delegated Legislation: Classification of Administrative Functions; Legislative Functions; Quasi-Judicial Functions; Administrative Functions; Ministerial Functions; Delegated Legislation; Meaning of Delegated Legislation; Reasons for Growth of Delegated Legislation; Classification of Delegated Legislation; Judicial Control of Delegated Legislation; Legislative Control of Delegated Legislation; Procedural Control of Delegated Legislation

syllabus.Course Objectives: CO1: To introduce students to the meaning, nature, evolution and scope of Administrative Law. CO2: To examine the principles of Rule of Law, Separation of Powers and delegated legislation. CO3: To analyze administrative functions and judicial control of administrative actions. CO4: To develop understanding of natural justice, administrative discretion and constitutional remedies. CO5: To familiarize students with administrative tribunals, public corporations and liability of the State.
syllabus.Suggested Readings: Griffith and Street – Principles of Administrative Law; H.W.R. Wade – Administrative Law; De Smith – Judicial Review of Administrative Action; S.P. Sathe – Administrative Law; I.P. Massey – Administrative Law; Jain and Jain – Principles of Administrative Law; M.P. Jain – Indian Constitutional Law; C.K. Takwani – Lectures on Administrative Law; Basu – Administrative Law; V.N. Shukla – Constitution
syllabus.Suggested Case Laws: A.K. Kraipak v Union of India; Maneka Gandhi v Union of India; Ridge v Baldwin; Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation; State of Punjab v Gurdial Singh; E.P. Royappa v State of Tamil Nadu; Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service; Barium Chemicals Ltd v Company Law Board; S.P. Gupta v Union of India; Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation
syllabus.Course Learning Outcomes: CO1: Explain the meaning, scope and development of Administrative Law. CO2: Analyze principles relating to Rule of Law, Separation of Powers and delegated legislation. CO3: Examine administrative functions and mechanisms of judicial review of administrative action. CO4: Apply principles of natural justice and constitutional remedies in administrative law disputes. CO5: Evaluate the role of administrative tribunals, public authorities and State liability in modern governance.

msData.name: LAW OF BANKING AND NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS

Course Content.UNIT I: Introduction to Banking Law: History of Banking Regulation Act; Salient Features of Banking Regulation Act; Banking Business and its Importance; Different Kinds of Banking; Impact of Information Technology on Banking
Course Content.UNIT V: Banking Securities and Recovery Mechanisms: Banker’s Lien; Right of Set Off; Advances by Banks; Pledge; Land as Security; Stocks and Shares as Security; Life Policies; Documents of Title to Goods; Bank Guarantees; Letters of Credit. Recovery of Bank Loans: SARFAESI Act, 2002; Recovery of Debts; Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT); Jurisdiction and Powers of DRT
Course Content.UNIT II: Relationship between Banker and Customer: Banker and Customer Relationship; Debtor and Creditor Relationship; Fiduciary Relationship; Trustee and Beneficiary Relationship; Principal and Agent Relationship; Bailor and Bailee Relationship; Guarantor Relationship
Course Content.UNIT IV: Paying and Collecting Banker: Paying Banker: Duties of Paying Banker; Statutory Protection to Paying Banker; Rights and Obligations of Paying Banker. Collecting Banker: Duties of Collecting Banker; Statutory Protection to Collecting Banker; Rights and Obligations of Collecting Banker
Course Content.UNIT III: Negotiable Instruments: Cheques; Crossed Cheques; Account Payee Cheques; Banker’s Drafts; Dividend Warrants; Negotiable Instruments; Deemed Negotiable Instruments; Salient Features of Negotiable Instruments Act

syllabus.Course Objectives: CO1: To introduce students to banking laws, banking transactions and negotiable instruments in India. CO2: To explain the legal relationship between banker and customer and banking obligations. CO3: To develop understanding of negotiable instruments, cheques and banking operations. CO4: To analyze rights, duties and liabilities of paying and collecting bankers. CO5: To familiarize students with recovery mechanisms, banking securities and SARFAESI framework.
syllabus.Suggested Readings: Tannan – Banking Law and Practice in India; Avtar Singh – Negotiable Instruments; P.N. Varshney – Banking Law and Practice; Taxman – Law of Banking; B.R. Sharma and R.P. Nainta – Principles of Banking Law and Negotiable Instruments Act; Mukherjee – Banking Law and Practice; Bashyam and Adiga – Negotiable Instruments Act; S.R. Myneni – Law of Banking; Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Bare Act); SARFAESI Act, 2002 and Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Bare Acts)
syllabus.Suggested Case Laws: State Bank of India v Shyama Devi; Canara Bank v Canara Sales Corporation; Central Bank of India v Siriguppa Sugars and Chemicals Ltd; ICICI Bank v Official Liquidator of APS Star Industries Ltd; Mardia Chemicals Ltd v Union of India; Transcore v Union of India; Keshavlal Khemchand and Sons Pvt Ltd v Union of India; Laxmi Dyechem v State of Gujarat; Modi Cements Ltd v Kuchil Kumar Nandi; ICDS Ltd v Beena Shabeer
syllabus.Course Learning Outcomes: CO1: Explain the legal framework governing banking operations and negotiable instruments. CO2: Analyze legal relationships and obligations between bankers and customers. CO3: Examine legal provisions relating to negotiable instruments and banking transactions. CO4: Apply banking law principles relating to securities, guarantees and recovery proceedings. CO5: Evaluate legal remedies and regulatory mechanisms in banking and financial disputes.

Course Content.Unit-I: Introduction to Human Rights: Meaning and definition of Human Rights; Evolution of Human Rights; Human Rights and Domestic Jurisdiction; Classification of Human Rights; Third World Perspectives of Human Rights
Course Content.Unit-V: Human Rights Protection in India: Protection of Human Rights in India; Protection of Human Rights Act; National Human Rights Commission (NHRC); State Human Rights Commissions; Human Rights Courts in Districts
Course Content.Unit-II: United Nations and Human Rights: Adoption of Human Rights by the UN Charter; U.N. Commission on Human Rights; Universal Declaration of Human Rights; International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
Course Content.Unit-IV: International Human Rights Conventions: Genocide Convention; Convention against Torture; CEDAW; Child Rights Convention; Convention on Statelessness; Convention against Slavery; Convention on Refugees; International Conference on Human Rights, 1968; World Conference on Human Rights, 1993
Course Content.Unit-III: Regional Human Rights Systems: European Convention on Human Rights; American Convention on Human Rights; African Charter on Human Rights (Banjul Charter)

syllabus.Course Objectives: CO1: To introduce students to the concept, evolution and classification of Human Rights. CO2: To develop understanding regarding international human rights instruments and institutions. CO3: To familiarize students with regional and international human rights conventions. CO4: To impart knowledge relating to international protection mechanisms and conventions concerning human rights. CO5: To enable students to analyze the legal framework for protection of human rights in India.
syllabus.Suggested Readings: P.R. Gandhi (Ed.): Blackstone’s International Human Rights Documents, Universal Law Publishing Co., Delhi.; Richard B. Lillich and Frank C. Newman: International Human Rights – Problems of Law and Policy.; Frederick Quinn: Human Rights and You, OSCE/ODIHR, Warsaw.; T.S. Batra: Human Rights – A Critique, Metropolitan Book Company Pvt. Ltd., New Delhi.; Dr. U. Chandra: Human Rights, Allahabad Law Agency Publications, Allahabad.
syllabus.Suggested Case Laws: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan; D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal; Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation; People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India; ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla; Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration; Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi
syllabus.Course Learning Outcomes: CO1: Explain the meaning, evolution and classification of Human Rights. CO2: Apply principles of international human rights law and UN human rights instruments. CO3: Analyze regional and international conventions relating to protection of human rights. CO4: Examine international mechanisms for protection of vulnerable groups and prevention of human rights violations. CO5: Evaluate the role of human rights institutions and courts in protection of human rights in India.

msData.name: MOOT COURTS, OBSERVATION OF TRIAL, PRE-TRIAL PREPARATIONS AND INTERNSHIP

Course Content.Component-A: Moot Court Exercises: Participation in minimum three Moot Courts; Drafting of Memorials and Written Submissions; Summary of Facts; Framing of Issues; Legal Arguments and Citations; Prayer and Reliefs; Oral Advocacy Skills; Court Manners and Presentation Skills; Communication and Advocacy Techniques
Course Content.Component-B: Observation of Trial Proceedings: Observation of one Civil Trial; Observation of one Criminal Trial; Recording stages of trial proceedings; Court Procedures and Judicial Process; Role of Judge, Advocate and Court Staff; Maintenance of Court Observation Diary
Course Content.Component-C: Interviewing Techniques, Pre-Trial Preparation and Internship: Client Interviewing: Observation of Interview Sessions; Client Counselling Techniques; Recording Client Statements; Professional Ethics during Client Interaction. Pre-Trial Preparation: Preparation of Court Documents and Case Files; Filing Procedure of Suits and Petitions; Drafting Assistance and Documentation. Internship: Mandatory Internship for minimum 15 days; Maintenance of Internship Diary; Practical Exposure to Court and Legal Office Work
Course Content.Component-D: Viva-Voce: Viva-Voce on Moot Court Exercises; Viva on Trial Observation; Viva on Internship and Pre-Trial Preparation; Professional Communication Skills; Court Craft and Legal Ethics

syllabus.Course Objectives: CO1: To introduce students to practical advocacy skills through moot court exercises and court observation. CO2: To develop skills relating to legal research, memorial drafting and oral advocacy. CO3: To familiarize students with court procedures, trial processes and practical functioning of courts. CO4: To impart practical knowledge regarding client interviewing, pre-trial preparation and drafting of court documents. CO5: To enable students to acquire professional legal skills and practical exposure through internship and viva-voce training.
syllabus.Suggested Readings: Dr. Kailash Rai: Moot Court Pre-Trial Preparation and Participation in Trial Proceedings, Central Law Publication.; Amita Danda: Moot Court for Interactive Legal Education, Asia Law House, Hyderabad.; Blackstone’s: Books of Moots, Oxford University Press.; Mishra: Moot Court Pre-Trial Preparation and Participation in Trial Proceedings, Central Law Publication, Allahabad.; G.B. Reddy: Practical Advocacy of Law, Gogia Law Agency, Hyderabad.
syllabus.Suggested Case Laws: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India; Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan; Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation; D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal; A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras; Donoghue v. Stevenson; MC Mehta v. Union of India; State of Rajasthan v. Union of India; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
syllabus.Course Learning Outcomes: CO1: Explain the practical aspects of advocacy, moot court proceedings and court procedures. CO2: Apply legal research, drafting and oral advocacy skills in moot court exercises and memorial preparation. CO3: Analyze civil and criminal trial procedures through court observation and practical exposure. CO4: Demonstrate interviewing techniques, client counselling and pre-trial preparation skills during internship and practical training. CO5: Develop professional ethics, advocacy skills, communication abilities and practical legal competence through moot courts, internship and viva-voce.
